title: The Quarter We Can See
hookLine: the whole world, every star and ant, is one quarter of the cosmic person. why hindus see god in nature without calling nature all of god
carry: god fills the world and is still more
tomorrow: what was the world made from?
last: A THOUSAND HEADS, AND TEN FINGERS MORE.

lines: THE COWORKER WHO FIXES THE PRINTER.
cards: Someone you've worked beside for years, the one who fixes the printer and remembers birthdays, stands up at a wedding and sings. The room goes quiet, because the voice is extraordinary. You had no idea.
You knew a real part of this person, nothing fake about it. But it was a part, and not the larger one. The Purusha Sukta's third verse does something like that with the whole world.
It takes everything that exists, every star and ant and city, and says: this is the part of him you've met.

teach.h: SUCH IS HIS GREATNESS, AND MORE.
teach.b: Verse three: such is his greatness, and the Purusha is greater still. Then a proportion. Pado asya vishva bhutani.
A quarter of him is all beings.
Pada means a foot, and also a quarter.
Everything that lives and dies is one quarter. Three quarters of him, the verse says, are immortal, in heaven. Verse four goes on.
With three quarters the Purusha rose up. The one quarter came to be here, again and again, and from it he spread out into what eats and what doesn't: the hungry sparrow and the stone.
So the world, for all its size, is the smaller share. Every galaxy, every person, is truly his, and still only the part that came down. Later Hindu texts keep this shape.
In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna tells Arjuna he holds up this whole universe with a single fragment of himself.

teach.h: IN GOD, AND GOD IS MORE.
teach.b: Scholars sometimes call this panentheism: everything is in God, and God is more than everything. It's why a Hindu can bow to a river, a tree, a cow, a teacher, and still pray to a God no river could hold.
So if someone says Hindus just worship nature, the oldest layer of the Veda answers: nature is sacred because it's his, and it's the quarter we can see.

how: Hindu teachers cite the Purusha Sukta's 'a quarter of him is all beings' and the Gita's 'a single fragment' when speaking of the divine as present in the world and also beyond it; the hymn is recited in Vedic chanting.

o: a hymn dividing the year into four seasons
a prayer to the god who rules a fourth of heaven
the hymn of the cosmic person, the world his quarter

games.q: verses three and four — tap the pairs.

s: the hymn says the world is the whole of the Purusha
it says all beings are one quarter of him, and three quarters are immortal in heaven.
pada can mean both a foot and a quarter
the same word serves for both, and here it means a quarter.
the Gita has a similar picture
Krishna says he holds up the whole universe with a single fragment of himself.

games.q: a friend says, "so Hindus just worship nature." what does the Purusha Sukta's proportion answer?
o: right: the world is all there is of God
the world is sacred, but it's one quarter; three quarters are beyond
the world has nothing to do with God
games.why: pado asya vishva bhutani: a quarter of him is all beings, three quarters immortal in heaven. God fills the world and is still more.

practice: Look at one living thing near you, a plant, a pet, the sky in a window, or picture one. Let it be sacred, part of the quarter that came down, and touch your hands together toward it.
Then close your eyes and rest in what's beyond it, the three quarters no eye has seen. If you pray, pray to the One who is more; if you don't, simply rest in the more.

wordCard.voice: The Purusha Sukta. In its third and fourth verses, all beings are one quarter of the Purusha, and three quarters are immortal in heaven.

orig.note: Sanskrit: a foot, and a quarter. In Rig Veda 10.90.3, all beings are one pada of the Purusha.

carryVoice: Your line: God fills the world, and is still more. The whole world is the quarter that came down. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Rig Veda 10.90.3 (such is his greatness, and the Purusha is greater still; a quarter of him is all beings, three quarters immortal in heaven)
Rig Veda 10.90.4 (with three quarters he rose up; a quarter came to be here again, and from it he spread out into what eats and what does not)
